strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and clearly articulated gap in the RL-for-AFC literature: existing benchmarks depend on external, often brittle CFD solver couplings and provide only partial differentiability, 3D, and MARL support; FluidGym is the first to unify all four properties in a single PyTorch codebase.

Substantial engineering and experimental effort: 13 environments across 4 canonical flow classes (cylinder, RBC, airfoil, TCF), 3 difficulty levels, single- and multi-agent variants, standardized train/val/test splits, and over 16k GPU hours of baseline experiments with PPO/SAC/MA-PPO/MA-SAC.

Careful numerical validation of the underlying solver and each environment against prior published results (drag coefficients, Nusselt numbers, lift/drag ratios, opposition-control drag reduction), which supports the correctness of the benchmark's physics.

The differentiability of the framework is put to concrete use via a proof-of-concept differentiable MPC controller that achieves competitive drag reduction purely from reward gradients, illustrating a genuinely novel capability relative to prior AFC benchmarks.

Transfer-learning studies (2D→3D policy transfer, small→large domain transfer for TCF) provide additional scientific insight beyond a pure software contribution, showing that MARL policies can generalize across dimensionality and domain size.

Extensive, well-organized supplementary material (formal MDP/POMDP definitions, environment specifications, hyperparameters, per-environment training curves, qualitative flow visualizations) supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Statistical robustness is limited by design: only 5 seeds (3 for 3D cylinder/airfoil) are used, which the paper itself flags as insufficient in the related-work critique of prior AFC studies (citing Henderson et al. 2018; Agarwal et al. 2021); some reported performance differences (e.g., MA-PPO vs MA-SAC) explicitly fall within confidence intervals, weakening the strength of the comparative claims.

Baselines are evaluated with default Stable-Baselines3 hyperparameters rather than tuned per environment, which the authors acknowledge may not reflect each algorithm's true achievable performance and could bias comparisons (e.g., the consistent SAC-over-PPO finding could partly be an artifact of untuned PPO).

The differentiability angle, a central selling point, is only lightly exercised: D-MPC is demonstrated on a single simple 2D cylinder environment with a plain gradient-ascent controller, and no comparison is made with the differentiable-RL methods (Xu et al. 2022; Xing et al. 2025) that motivated the benchmark's design, leaving the practical value of full differentiability for RL acceleration largely unvalidated.

"Plug-and-play" and standalone claims are somewhat overstated given the hard requirement for a CUDA-enabled GPU with custom kernels (no CPU fallback), which limits accessibility relative to some existing CFD-coupled benchmarks that can (slowly) run on CPU.

The core contribution is primarily an engineering/integration effort (a benchmark suite) rather than a new algorithmic or scientific method; while valuable to the community, the methodological novelty is modest, and the significance depends heavily on future community adoption, which cannot yet be assessed.

Some individual results appear inconsistent or under-analyzed (e.g., SAC yielding negative drag reduction relative to baseflow on CylinderJet3D-hard), and the paper does not deeply discuss failure modes or provide statistical significance testing between algorithms beyond confidence intervals in aggregate plots.

No direct empirical comparison (e.g., running the same algorithm/environment pair) against existing benchmarks such as HydroGym is provided to substantiate claims of superior usability or performance, so the comparative advantages in Table 1 rest on qualitative feature checklists rather than head-to-head evidence.

strengths: The paper fills a genuine gap: a standalone, PyTorch-native, GPU-accelerated RL benchmark for active flow control that removes dependency on external CFD solvers, which is a real pain point highlighted convincingly in the related-work survey and Table 1.

Reasonably comprehensive scope on paper: 13 named environments across 4 flow configurations (cylinder, Rayleigh-Bénard convection, airfoil, turbulent channel flow), spanning 2D/3D and SARL/MARL settings with 3 difficulty levels each.

Solver validation effort (Appendix B.3) compares uncontrolled baseline statistics (drag/lift coefficients, Nusselt numbers, wall shear stress) against prior published results, lending some credibility to the simulation fidelity.

Differentiability is leveraged for a proof-of-concept D-MPC controller that achieves drag reduction purely from reward gradients, illustrating a capability unique relative to prior non-differentiable benchmarks.

Transfer-learning experiments (2D→3D policy transfer, small→large channel domain transfer) are a nice addition that goes beyond simple baseline training and yields some interesting (if under-explained) findings about MARL's spatial generalization.
Public release of code, environments, datasets, and trained models supports reproducibility and community adoption in principle.
weaknesses: Significant contradiction between claims and actual experiments: the abstract/intro claims 'an extensive experimental study covering all FluidGym environments and difficulty levels,' yet Table 7 shows zero GPU hours for RBC2D-wide, RBC3D-wide, Airfoil3D-medium/hard, and both TCF-bottom variants — roughly half of the advertised 13 environments were never actually run in this study. This undermines the central 'comprehensive benchmark' claim.

Statistical rigor is weak relative to the paper's own stated motivation (criticizing prior work for using too few seeds). Only 5 seeds (3 for costly 3D cases) are used, and many of the headline comparisons (e.g., 'SAC reliably outperforms PPO') rest on overlapping confidence intervals in Figure 4 and unreported variance in Tables 8–11, so the strength of these claims is not well supported.

The differentiability selling point — arguably the paper's main technical novelty — is only demonstrated with a toy D-MPC baseline on a single simple 2D cylinder environment with no comparison to actual differentiable RL methods (e.g., the very methods cited as motivation, Xing et al. 2025; Lagemann et al. 2025b) or systematic analysis of when/why gradients help over model-free RL.

Baselines are run with default Stable-Baselines3 hyperparameters without any tuning, which is itself a methodological shortcut the paper criticizes other works for; this weakens confidence that the reported PPO vs. SAC comparisons reflect each algorithm's true potential rather than an artifact of hyperparameter mismatch.

Several reported outcomes are non-monotonic or counterintuitive (e.g., SAC achieving negative 'drag reduction' at CylinderJet3D-hard; MA-SAC performing worse than baseflow at RBC2D-hard) without sufficient discussion or diagnosis, raising questions about training stability/convergence at scale.

Numerical validation shows nontrivial deviations from established literature values (e.g., ~3.8% drag coefficient deviation for cylinder flow, ~14–17% discrepancy in airfoil lift/drag relative to Wang et al.), with explanations (different domain lengths/boundary conditions) that are plausible but not rigorously verified, leaving open questions about whether the environments reproduce the intended physical regimes faithfully.

The 'plug-and-play' and accessibility framing is undercut by the hard CUDA-only requirement (custom CUDA kernels, no CPU fallback), which is a real barrier for many potential users and somewhat at odds with the paper's stated goal of lowering the barrier to entry.

No direct quantitative cross-validation against existing benchmarks (e.g., running comparable tasks in HydroGym or DRLinFluids to show consistent RL performance/conclusions) — the comparison in Table 1 is purely feature-based rather than empirically substantiated.

strengths: Addresses a genuine, well-documented gap in the RL-for-AFC literature: existing benchmarks require external CFD solvers, are only partially differentiable, and offer limited 3D/MARL support; FluidGym is the first to unify all these properties in a single PyTorch stack.

Very extensive empirical study: 13 environments (4 flow configurations × multiple difficulty levels/variants), both SARL and MARL settings, 5 seeds for most environments (3 for the most expensive 3D cases), totaling >16k GPU hours, with all code, data, and trained models publicly released.

Good methodological rigor relative to prior AFC-RL work: uses standardized train/val/test splits with multiple initial conditions, reports IQM/performance profiles with bootstrapped confidence intervals following Agarwal et al. (2021), directly addressing the evaluation pitfalls the paper itself identifies in related work.

Solver/environment validation against prior published results (drag coefficients, Nusselt numbers, opposition-control drag reduction) lends credibility to the physical fidelity of the implemented environments.

The transfer-learning experiments (2D→3D policy transfer, small-to-large-domain transfer in MARL) are a nice value-added analysis beyond a standard benchmark paper and yield interesting, if preliminary, insights about spatial/dimensional generalization.
The differentiability of the framework is demonstrated concretely via a gradient-only D-MPC baseline, illustrating a genuinely new capability that prior non-differentiable benchmarks cannot offer.
weaknesses: The core contribution is an engineering/infrastructure artifact rather than new algorithmic or scientific insight; the RL findings reported (SAC generally outperforms PPO, MARL variants are comparable) mostly confirm well-known trends rather than revealing new understanding.

The differentiability selling point — argued at length in the introduction as enabling DPC and differentiable RL methods that 'accelerate training and outperform classical RL' — is only lightly validated via a single-environment D-MPC proof of concept; no comparison to differentiable RL methods (e.g., the cited Xing et al. 2025, Lagemann et al. 2025b) is actually performed, so the central claimed advantage over existing benchmarks is underexplored empirically.

All RL baselines use default Stable-Baselines3 hyperparameters without tuning, which the authors acknowledge may not reflect each algorithm's true capability; this weakens the reliability of cross-algorithm comparisons that the paper otherwise emphasizes as a main contribution (fair, standardized comparison).

Statistical robustness is still limited (3–5 seeds), which is explicitly flagged by the authors as a limitation but remains a real constraint on the strength of comparative claims, especially given known RL seed variance issues the paper itself cites (Henderson et al., 2018).

The benchmark's physical fidelity and extensibility depend entirely on a concurrently/recently published, GPU-specific CUDA solver (PICT, Franz et al. 2026) that lacks CPU support, which may limit accessibility, long-term community adoption, and independent scrutiny of the solver outside the same research group.

Several reported results are inconsistent or under-discussed (e.g., negative drag reduction for SAC on CylinderJet3D-hard, non-monotonic MARL vs SARL performance across difficulty levels), and the paper offers only high-level qualitative explanations without deeper diagnostic analysis.

Aggregating heterogeneous environments into single performance profiles/IQM scores (Fig. 4) can obscure environment-specific behavior and makes it harder to assess true algorithmic significance versus benchmark-specific artifacts.

strengths: Fills a genuine and well-articulated gap in the AFC-RL benchmarking landscape: FluidGym is the first benchmark that is simultaneously standalone (no external CFD dependency), fully differentiable across all environments, natively supports MARL, and includes high-fidelity 3D tasks — Table 1 makes this comparative positioning against DRLinFluids, drlFoam, DRLFluent, Gym-preCICE, Beacon, and HydroGym clear and convincing.

Substantial engineering and experimental effort: 13 environments across 4 flow classes (cylinder, RBC, airfoil, channel flow) with 3 difficulty levels each, evaluated with PPO, SAC, MA-PPO, MA-SAC, DPC, and TD-MPC using 5 seeds and 10 test episodes per configuration, totaling >25k GPU hours — a genuinely large-scale benchmarking study rarely seen in this subfield.

Reasonable physical validation of environments against published values (drag coefficients, Nusselt numbers, lift/drag ratios, opposition-control drag reduction), including a grid refinement study for RBC, which increases confidence that the simulations are not just fast but physically sound.

Appropriate statistical methodology for RL evaluation (performance profiles, IQM scores, bootstrap confidence intervals following Agarwal et al. 2021), a rarity in the AFC-RL literature that the paper itself criticizes for weak evaluation practices.

Interesting emergent scientific findings beyond pure benchmarking: coordinated MARL behavior forming convection rolls in 3D RBC, successful 2D→3D and small→large domain policy transfer, and demonstration of DPC's sample-efficiency advantage via full differentiability.

Strong transparency and reproducibility support: extensive appendices detailing numerical setups, hyperparameters, domain configurations, and public release of code, environments, datasets, and trained models.
weaknesses: Only 5 random seeds are used, which the authors themselves acknowledge limits the statistical robustness of algorithm comparisons; several reported differences (e.g., MA-SAC vs. MA-PPO) lie within overlapping confidence intervals, undermining some of the paper's comparative claims (e.g., 'SAC reliably outperforms PPO').

All RL baselines use default Stable-Baselines3 hyperparameters without tuning; this promotes comparability but means conclusions about relative algorithm performance may reflect hyperparameter mismatch rather than genuine algorithmic superiority, weakening claims made in Sections 4.2 and 4.6.

The core differentiability contribution—arguably the paper's main technical novelty over HydroGym/Beacon—is only exercised via DPC and TD-MPC on two simple 2D environments (CylinderJet2D, RBC2D); no differentiable-RL hybrid methods (despite being motivated at length in the intro/related work) are actually evaluated, and DPC training reportedly degraded and had to be stopped early, raising doubts about its practical robustness even in the paper's own limited demonstration.

The environments themselves are largely reimplementations of well-established AFC tasks from prior literature (cylinder wake, RBC, airfoil, channel flow); the paper's originality lies primarily in software/systems integration rather than new scientific tasks, algorithms, or insights, which may limit its research (as opposed to infrastructure) contribution.

Reliance on a single, custom, GPU-only PICT solver as the sole backend is a potential adoption risk and single point of failure; no CPU fallback exists, and the solver's independent validation is relatively recent and not extensively cross-checked against multiple established codes beyond the reported comparisons.

Some reward-shaping and MARL design choices (e.g., local/global reward weighting β=0.8, action smoothing parameter α=0.1) are adopted from prior single-paper precedents without ablation, so their influence on the reported comparative results is unclear.

Occasional negative or counter-intuitive results (e.g., SAC yielding negative drag reduction on CylinderJet3D-hard) are reported without deeper analysis or discussion of failure modes, leaving open questions about environment difficulty calibration or training instability at scale.

strengths: Addresses a real and well-documented problem in the AFC-RL literature: fragmented, hard-to-reproduce experimental setups, heavy dependence on brittle external CFD/coupling stacks, and weak statistical practice (few seeds, reward normalization issues, training/test leakage) that the authors carefully document with specific citations.

Substantial engineering effort: 13 standardized environments across 4 flow classes (cylinder, RBC, airfoil, TCF), 3 difficulty levels, SARL and MARL interfaces, >25k GPU hours of experiments, public release of code/datasets/trained models.

Reasonably rigorous evaluation protocol relative to much prior AFC-RL work: 5 seeds, held-out train/val/test initial-condition splits, performance profiles and IQM scores following Agarwal et al. (2021) with bootstrap confidence intervals, rather than single uncontrolled-baseline comparisons common in the field.

Useful supplementary validation of the underlying solver/environments against previously published drag coefficients, Nusselt numbers, and opposition-control drag reduction, which helps establish numerical credibility.

Interesting transfer-learning studies (2D→3D policy transfer, small→large-domain MARL transfer) and emergent multi-agent coordination results (two convection rolls in RBC3D) that illustrate some of the benchmark's unique capabilities (MARL + 3D + differentiability).
weaknesses: The headline selling point — full differentiability enabling gradient-based control — is only demonstrated on two small, simple environments (CylinderJet2D, RBC2D) out of 13, and even there DPC training "degraded" and had to be stopped early; this is a thin and somewhat negative demonstration of the paper's most distinctive claimed contribution relative to prior benchmarks (Table 1).

The "no external solver" claim is largely a packaging distinction: FluidGym still depends entirely on a separate, non-trivial, CUDA-kernel-based CFD solver (PICT) that is not CPU-compatible, which undercuts the "plug-and-play"/accessibility framing for non-GPU or non-expert users, a limitation the paper itself concedes only briefly.

Algorithm comparisons rely exclusively on off-the-shelf default SB3 hyperparameters (explicitly acknowledged as a limitation), which is in tension with the paper's stated goal of enabling fair, systematic comparison of control methods; conclusions such as "SAC outperforms PPO" are unsurprising and not clearly disentangled from hyperparameter choice.

Only 5 random seeds are used despite the paper's own critique that few-seed evaluation is a major reproducibility weakness in the field (Henderson et al., Agarwal et al.); many reported differences (e.g., MA-PPO vs MA-SAC) are stated to lie within confidence intervals, limiting the strength of the benchmark's own conclusions.

Despite the introduction explicitly flagging that "more advanced continuous-control methods... remain largely unexplored in AFC," the paper's own baseline suite does not include any such methods (e.g., TD3, distributional or hypergraph-action methods cited), so this gap identified as motivation is not actually filled.

The scientific contribution beyond infrastructure is modest: findings (SAC > PPO, PPO benefiting more from MARL's effective sample multiplication, 2D→3D transfer sometimes working) are plausible but not deeply analyzed or surprising, and the paper reads primarily as a software/infrastructure release rather than new knowledge about flow control or RL algorithms.

Validation discrepancies versus prior literature (e.g., ~3.8% cylinder drag deviation, airfoil domain-length mismatch) are acknowledged but not fully resolved, leaving some uncertainty about how directly FluidGym results compare to the broader AFC literature it aims to unify.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: the paper carefully reviews the heterogeneous evaluation practices in RL-for-AFC literature (sparse seeds, inconsistent initial conditions, PPO-only baselines) and designs FluidGym directly to address these documented gaps, with a convincing comparison table against six prior benchmarks.

Genuine technical novelty as the first standalone (no external CFD solver), fully end-to-end differentiable AFC benchmark with native multi-agent support and 3D high-fidelity tasks, built on a single PyTorch stack (PICT solver), which removes a major practical adoption barrier compared to OpenFOAM/Fluent/FEniCS/m-AIA-coupled alternatives.

Broad and carefully engineered environment suite (13 environments across 4 flow classes, 3 difficulty levels, SARL/MARL variants, standardized train/val/test splits with reproducible RNG seeding) accompanied by non-trivial numerical validation against established literature values (cylinder drag, RBC Nusselt number grid-refinement study, airfoil lift/drag, channel-flow opposition control).

Extensive empirical study (>25k GPU hours, 5 seeds, 10 test episodes per setting) covering PPO, SAC, their multi-agent variants, DPC, and TD-MPC, including rigorous statistical reporting via performance profiles and IQM scores (Agarwal et al., 2021 style), plus interesting secondary analyses: emergent multi-agent coordination in 3D RBC, 2D→3D and small→large domain transfer, and wall-clock runtime comparisons across algorithms.

Honest and specific limitations/future-work section (seed count, CUDA dependency, limited DPC scope, default hyperparameters) that does not overstate the contribution, alongside a reasonable impact statement.
Public release of code, environments, datasets, and trained models is promised, which if delivered would substantially lower barriers to entry and support reproducibility in this fragmented subfield.
weaknesses: Statistical robustness remains limited (5 seeds) despite the paper's own critique of prior work for exactly this issue; while computational cost is a legitimate constraint, some comparative claims (e.g., SAC vs PPO, MA-PPO vs MA-SAC) rest on differences that the paper itself notes partially overlap with confidence intervals.

The gradient-based control demonstration (DPC) and TD-MPC, which are central to the "fully differentiable" selling point, are only evaluated on two simple 2D environments (CylinderJet2D, RBC2D); the claimed advantage of differentiability for scaling to complex 3D/MARL settings is therefore not empirically demonstrated, leaving a gap between the framework's stated capability and the evidence provided.

Hard dependency on CUDA-enabled GPUs with custom kernels limits the "plug-and-play" and accessibility claims for users without GPU access, somewhat undercutting the stated goal of lowering barriers to entry relative to CPU-friendly solvers.

Baselines use default Stable-Baselines3 hyperparameters without tuning (aside from a limited PPO network-size ablation), so reported algorithm comparisons may not reflect each method's best achievable performance, which could affect the benchmark's conclusions about algorithmic ranking.

Some reported results are weak or negative (e.g., SAC achieving negative drag reduction on CylinderJet3D-hard), which, while honestly reported, suggests that several of the harder 3D/MARL tasks are not yet well-solved by any baseline, limiting the immediate utility of the benchmark for establishing meaningful state-of-the-art comparisons at the hardest difficulty tiers.

As a new, custom solver (PICT) underlying all environments, the correctness and numerical fidelity rely on a validation study that, while reasonable, is relatively brief (single reference comparisons per environment class) relative to the complexity and novelty of the underlying CFD implementation.
